headline.main: Finland Confronts Its WWII History: "If You Only Knew How Many Jews I Have Shot"
headline.social: Finland Confronts Its WWII History: "If You Only Knew How Many Jews I Have Shot"

intro: Hundreds of Finns fought with the German Waffen-SS in Ukraine during World War II. New research shows that many of them were convinced Nazis and may have committed atrocities. The finding has triggered a debate in Finland.
text:
Tauno Aarni had only been in Sweden for a couple of weeks before he started talking. From Finland, Aarni had found shelter in a refugee camp in the Swedish port city of Gävle because he, as an anti-communist, allegedly faced persecution back home.
In late November 1944, Aarni spoke with a police officer who he thought shared his views on Judaism. Jews, he told the police officer, cannot be seen as humans. He continued with a sentence that would prove problematic for him: "If you only knew how many Jews I have shot.”
It may not have just been empty talk. Aarni was one of 1,408 Finnish men who volunteered to serve in Nazi Germany’s Waffen-SS during World War II and took part in Hitler’s campaign of extermination against the Soviet Union. They were integrated into the Wiking Division, a unit that committed dozens of massacres in Ukraine. The Swedish police kept an eye on Aarni, the purported refugee, and interrogated him several times after the war came to an end.
Eighty years later, Finnish historian André Swanström examined the interrogation transcripts and other sources. His results will be published in spring in the journal Holocaust and Genocide Studies, the first time they will appear in English. And they are likely to intensify an already controversial discussion.
For the last several years, a debate has been swelling in Finland over the country’s cooperation with Nazi Germany during World War II. In 1941, the country joined the Nazi attack on the Soviet Union as "brothers-in-arms.” Was it a form of preventative self-defense? Or did it make Finland an accomplice to the crimes committed by the Nazis?
The Finnish volunteers in the Waffen-SS are a particular focus of this delayed reappraisal. Researchers have found evidence that some of them very likely participated in atrocities committed in Ukraine.
But some elements of Finnish society want to hear nothing about it and see the volunteers as Finnish patriots - particularly supporters of the right-wing populist party Perussuomalaiset (formerly known as the True Finns but now called the Finns Party), but also the military and others on the right of the political spectrum. According to the commonly accepted narrative, the Finnish SS members had nothing to do with war crimes and the Holocaust – or, if they did, they were forced to participate against their will.
Swanström’s research points to a different conclusion. "Ideology was present as a driving force all along: from recruitment to the entire chain of command leading to pulling the trigger," he writes in a research paper. "There is," he says, "much to indicate that some of the Finnish volunteers were willing executioners in the Holocaust.”
A Symbol of Rapprochement
Finland played a special role in the history of World War II. In the non-aggression pact (often referred to as the "Hitler-Stalin Pact”) signed in August 1939 by the German "Führer” Adolf Hitler and the Soviet dictator Josef Stalin, Finland was assigned to the Soviet sphere of influence in a secret protocol attached to the deal. When Moscow’s Red Army attacked Finland a short time later, the Finns blocked the advance of the seemingly superior enemy in the Winter War. In March 1940, Helsinki concluded a peace deal with Moscow, with Finland ceding its part of Karelia and other territories to the Soviets.
Helsinki, however, didn’t believe that the harmony between Hitler and Stalin would last very long. The government believed it would have to choose one side or the other so as not to be trapped between the two great powers. The country chose Nazi Germany.
Finland began negotiating with Germany in August 1940 over arms deliveries. In return, the Germans would receive permission to attack the Soviet Union from Finnish territory. Soon, Finnish units also began cropping up in German war plans. The volunteer SS battalion was to be a symbol of rapprochement.
Formally, the Waffen-SS was independent from the Wehrmacht, as Nazi Germany’s military was known. It was commanded by Reichsführer SS Heinrich Himmler, who saw the SS as an elite force made up of ideologically reliable party loyalists.
Himmler recruited volunteers for the SS in other European countries as well, an attempt to demonstrate to the world how broad support was for the Nazi’s "anti-Bolshevist” policies. In January 1941, Hitler permitted Himmler to begin recruiting Finns.
Until recently, leading Finnish historians had argued that the volunteers were primarily non-politically minded boys of school age. Almost half of them, after all, were under 20 years old. The vast majority of them, they argued, joined the SS out of patriotism and the search for adventure. Swanström’s research has disproved this myth.
Twenty-eight men came to the recruitment office on the very first day, April 21, 1941. Their political leanings were noted on their application forms and seven named the fascist party Isänmaallinen Kansanliike (Patriotic People’s Movement), known for their uniforms of black shirts and blue ties. Four others belonged to a Swedish-speaking Nazi group whose leader published the anti-Semitic conspiracy narrative "The Protocols of the Elders of Zion.”
Another four volunteers, including Aarni, identified with other, smaller Nazi parties. Two more entered their preference as "anti-Semitic.” Eleven of the young men named moderate right-wing parties or indicated no political leanings. "Some of the most prominent Nazis among the Finnish SS men were the first to be recruited,” Swanström notes.
More right-wing radicals applied later. In total, 46 percent of all recruits supported organizations considered today to have been fascist. Nobody was rejected for being too extreme. The SS even accepted one Nazi who was actually too short, and another who was too old. Some of the Finnish SS members later said that recruiters had entered their party preferences against their will or without their knowledge. Swanström considers such claims to be disingenuous.
Backup for the Einsatzgruppen
On June 22, 1941, Hitler broke the non-aggression pact with Stalin and attacked the Soviet Union. Alongside the Germans, troops from Finland, Denmark, the Netherlands and Norway also fought in the SS Wiking Division. All of them had sworn an oath to the "Führer.”
The division, 19,000-strong initially, moved through Ukraine to the southeast. The motto, as the troops well knew, was: "The SS takes no prisoners.” Red Army soldiers who surrendered were frequently shot on the spot. The division was similarly merciless with the Jewish population. In the town of Zboriv, they are thought to have participated in the slaughter of 600 Jews that July. They also provided occasional support to the Einsatzgruppen, the special task forces that systematically murdered Jews, Roma and communists.
In this early phase in the war of extermination, 400 Finns were distributed among various units in the division. In late 1941, another 800 volunteers joined them, forming a battalion of their own. The division advanced all the way to the Caucasus before retreating to the other side of Russia’s Don River following the German defeat in Stalingrad.
In summer 1943, the Finnish government brought the SS volunteers back home. The official justification was that their two-year service contracts had expired. In reality, though, with expectations growing that the Nazis might lose the war, the Finns were eager to distance themselves from their erstwhile "brothers-in-arms.”
In 1944, the Finnish government concluded a separate peace deal with Stalin. Finland was required to cede territory to the Soviet Union, pay reparations and drive the Germans out of Lapland. All "fascist” organizations were banned, including the veterans club of the SS volunteers. Some, like Tauno Aarni, fled to Sweden.
After his careless remarks in the refugee camp, Aarni continually changed his story. He first told the police that he only shot at prisoners of war who happened to be Jewish. He then said that he had shot at Jewish members of the Red Army in self-defense. Later, he spoke of a mercy killing of a wounded Jew on the side of the road.
Finally, he denied killing any Jews at all and claimed that he was disgusted by the atrocities and by the Nazi ideology. Yet according to the files, he voluntarily attended a training course for the Hitler Youth in Garmisch-Partenkirchen after the Finnish SS battalion had been disbanded.
The Swedish authorities didn’t pursue the case despite the contradictory statements. Aarni received Swedish citizenship, started calling himself Teddy, got married and opened a photo studio. He taught well-known photographers and later moderated a television show.
Finland also soon lost interest in the former SS members. The country had defended its independence, though it aligned its foreign policy with that of the Soviet Union, and it was eager to avoid angering Moscow by admitting to having participated in the German war of extermination, which is thought to have cost the lives of 25 million Soviet citizens.
Finnish historians arrived at the formulation that Finland had waged a "separate war” against the Soviet Union. The SS volunteers, according to this narrative, fought just as honorably and independently as normal Finnish soldiers – just elsewhere.
It was only in 1968 that a historian looked into the Finnish SS volunteers. He pronounced them innocent of war crimes and of harboring Nazi sympathies, setting the tone for decades to come. The study had been funded by the newly founded federation of Finnish SS veterans called Brother Aid Heritage Association.
Some SS veterans were also rehabilitated in West Germany. Chancellor Konrad Adenauer, Germany’s first postwar leader, called them "soldiers like any others” in 1952. It was only in the 1980s that studies revealed the narrative of a "clean” Waffen-SS to be a myth. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, German historians comprehensively documented the massacres perpetrated by the Wiking Division in Ukraine.
Roughly concurrently, historians in Denmark and Sweden conducted research into volunteers from their countries. Norwegian studies followed. The results: Many of the volunteers harbored sympathies for the Nazis and some had participated in war crimes.
A Debate in Finland
In Finland, research into their own SS volunteers only got started in 2017. That year, Swanström, who is actually a church historian, began leafing through the correspondence of a military chaplain. In one letter, a group from the Wiking Division’s vehicle maintenance company asked the chaplain to lobby for their transfer to the front. One of the arguments set forth in the letter: "Poorer shooting skills than ours are enough for executing Jews."
Swanström saw it as proof that the letter’s signatories had participated in murdering Jews, a theory he published in the form of a blog post. "The reaction was fierce,” he says. "My email inbox was full of threats and insults.”
Critics from the academic community charged that Swanström had misinterpreted the letter, saying that the reference to executing Jews may have merely been an invented example or a bit of dark humor.
In 2018, the Prime Minister's Office commissioned a study by the National Archives of Finland. That study concluded that at least five Finns had very likely participated in atrocities. The study’s author estimates that Finnish volunteers murdered dozens of civilians and hundreds of prisoners of war.
Not everyone was impressed. Two retired colonels from the Finnish army wrote a letter to the editor in which they claimed that the study harmed the reputation of the dead. The defense minister at the time, who was a former member of the right-wing True Finns, wrote on his blog: "I believe it is unjust to cast the shadow of suspicion upon them without proof.”
Regarding the motives driving the SS volunteers, the National Archives study repeated the narrative of "politically inexperienced” men. Yet the journals kept be the SS members provide insight into their views on the Eastern Front. One noted almost in passing: "Four Jews were shot” – but the passive voice in Finnish can also be used for active sentences in the first-person plural. Another SS member captioned a photo with "Jew hunting.” A third wrote about a Soviet political commissioner who had apparently been executed: "The only thing he needed was 60 cm of soil on top (of) his snout.”
These statements, Swanström suspects, are possibly just the "tip of the iceberg.” He now wants to determine in a new study the degree to which the SS volunteers were driven by ideology. Those who keep journals, he says, tend to sugarcoat their accounts of events. On top of that, he points out, the volunteers burned numerous notebooks in 1944 before the police had a chance to confiscate them.
The historian expects that he will again be vilified for his paper once it is published in the spring. He says that the societal climate in Finland had deteriorated. The Finns Party, which has been back in government since 2023 and is strictly anti-Russian due to the country’s history, is trying to assert its revisionist view of history, Swanström claims. Recently, three government ministers from the party supported a motion to provide the SS veterans association with funding to conduct a counter-study.
On top of that, Swanström believes that the Russian invasion of Ukraine has reinforced conservative views of history. "Currently, old narratives of heroes and enemies are coming to the fore. The Russians are evil and their opponents are automatically good.” Swanström, though, also sees his work as a contribution to the defense of freedom. "We should not become a mirror image of the Russians, who reject any critical examination of their history.”
